title: Board Gender Diversity, Capital Structure, and Earnings Management: The Moderating Role of the Audit Committee
summary: Background: Recurring financial-reporting concerns in Indonesia and mixed prior evidence on the governance determinants of earnings management create a need to clarify when monitoring mechanisms constrain managerial reporting discretion. The study addresses the gap concerning whether audit committee meeting intensity conditions the relationships of board gender diversity and leverage with earnings management in an emerging-market consumer-sector setting. Objective: This study examines the associations of board gender diversity and capital structure with earnings management and tests audit committee meeting intensity as a moderator. Methods: The unit of analysis is 266 firm-year observations (133 consumer cyclical and consumer non-cyclical firms × 2 years) listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2023–2024 and selected purposively. A centered moderated regression was estimated in EViews 13 using Stubben’s discretionary-revenue measure and White cross-section robust standard errors. Results: Board gender diversity is negatively associated with earnings management (β = −0.0244; p = 0.0158), whereas leverage is positively associated with it (β = 0.0500; p < 0.001). The board-gender-diversity × audit-committee interaction is not significant (β = −0.0050; p = 0.2674), while the leverage × audit-committee interaction is negative and significant (β = −0.0218; p < 0.001). Conclusion: Audit committee meeting intensity appears to constrain leverage-related reporting pressure but does not significantly amplify the board-diversity pathway. The study contributes a conditional governance perspective in which monitoring mechanisms are matched to the source of reporting risk.

title: Omnichannel, Resilience, and Artificial Intelligence in the Supply Chain: a Bibliometric Analysis (2019–2026) and an Integrative Framework
summary: Objective: To map the intellectual and thematic structure of research on omnichannel (2019–2026) and, based on the identified themes, propose an integrative framework that connects omnichannel, supply chain resilience, and artificial intelligence (AI) without multiplying risks. Methods: A mixed-methods study combining bibliometric analysis—according to Donthu et al. (2021), based on a corpus of 2,869 journal articles extracted from the OpenAlex open-access database and selected using PRISMA—with performance analysis and scientific mapping, and the deductive construction of a conceptual framework based on the identified gaps. Results and Conclusion: Output grew from 99 articles (2019) to 813 (2025), totaling 26,161 citations; The United States, Indonesia, China, and India lead; and the thematic structure reveals a core focused on customer experience and channel integration, an axis centered on supply chain and logistics, and a cluster related to digital transformation, while AI and resilience remain emerging areas. In light of this gap, a four-layer framework is proposed—data sources, real-time integration, intelligence, and decision-making, under cross-functional governance—from which three management principles are derived: visibility with verification prior to automation; AI as augmentation, not replacement; and the primacy of competencies and coordination. Research Implications: The study provides a current overview of the field and a structured tool for managing the risks created by integration, with socio-environmental and sector-specific implications. Originality/Value: It links empirical evidence on the structure of the field to a conceptual framework, articulating omnichannel, resilience, and AI—which are usually treated in isolation—and reframing integration as a system that simultaneously mitigates and generates risks.

title: How Does Digital Innovation Drive Corporate Sustainability? A Systematic Literature Review
summary: This study systematically reviews recent empirical evidence on the relationship between digital innovation and corporate sustainability. Using the Scopus database, the review identified 231 articles through the search string (“digital” OR “digital innovation” OR “digitalization”) AND “corporate sustainability”. After applying inclusion criteria covering publications from 2023 to 2026, English-language journal articles, open access availability, and quantitative empirical design, 49 articles were retained for synthesis. The findings show that digital innovation is conceptualized through multiple forms, including digital transformation, digital finance, artificial intelligence, digital accounting, supply chain digitalization, digital leadership, executives’ digital attention, and digital–green integration. Most studies indicate that digital innovation positively contributes to ESG performance, corporate sustainability performance, sustainable development performance, and sustainability efficiency. However, the relationship is not automatic or universally linear. Its effect depends on mediating mechanisms such as green innovation, operational efficiency, financing access, information transparency, supply chain coordination, resource orchestration, and governance improvement. The review also identifies important boundary conditions, including digital maturity, organizational capability, leadership support, digital infrastructure, environmental regulation, and institutional quality. This study contributes by organizing fragmented empirical evidence into an integrated thematic framework and highlighting future research directions for global scholars examining digital transformation, ESG practices, and sustainability-oriented corporate strategy worldwide.

title: Shareholder connection network and corporate supply chain resilience: evidence from Chinese listed firms
summary: Purpose Supply chain resilience is crucial for firms navigating an increasingly volatile global environment, yet the factors that enhance it remain underexplored. Existing literature offers conflicting views on the role of shareholder connection networks, debating whether they foster governance synergy or promote competitive collusion. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data from Shanghai and Shenzhen A-share listed companies during the period 2012–2023, our study investigates the impact of the shareholder connection network as a circular-oriented relational intangible (circular intellectual capital) on supply chain resilience as a capability enabling circular transformation. Findings We find that such networks significantly enhance supply chain resilience. This positive effect operates through two primary channels: reducing operational risk and improving information disclosure quality relevant to inter-firm transparency, which in turn foster inter-firm trust and collaboration supporting regenerative, closed-loop supply chains. The impact is more pronounced among firms in growth or decline stages and in settings characterized by lower levels of marketization or less intense competition. Originality/value Our findings offer practical insights for managers to better understand the role of such networks in risk management and supply chain governance, aid firms in partner selection, and inform policymakers seeking to promote supply chain resilience and circular-oriented value creation through high-quality development.

title: Building Supply Chain Resilience in India’s Pharmaceutical Industry: API Import Dependence and the Production Linked Incentive Response
summary: India is a leading global supplier of generic medicines, yet its pharmaceutical industry depends heavily on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), key starting materials and drug intermediates, most of them from China. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed this vulnerability: prices of essential APIs rose sharply in early 2020, and India restricted exports of 26 APIs and formulations. This paper uses a qualitative case study design to examine how this vulnerability arose, how it was revealed by the pandemic, and how Indian policy has responded. Drawing on official trade data, parliamentary replies, government reports and the supply chain resilience literature, the study analyses the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for bulk drugs, the PLI scheme for pharmaceuticals and the Bulk Drug Parks scheme. The analysis shows that China accounted for roughly two-thirds of India’s bulk drug and intermediate imports by value between 2019–20 and 2022–23. The policy response has created new domestic capacity, and by early 2026 the government reported import substitution of about Rs 2,190 crore under the bulk drug scheme, which remains modest relative to total imports. The paper proposes a Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Resilience Framework and draws implications for managers and policymakers.

title: La performance de l'Investissement Socialement Responsable(ISR) au Maroc : Une analyse comparative au sein de la Bourse des Valeurs de Casablanca(BVC)
summary: RÉSUMÉ : L’Investissement socialement responsable (ISR) se considère comme la forme la plus dominante de la finance durable. Il est le reflet de la RSE au sein des marchés financiers. En effet, ce type d’investissement vise à réconcilier la performance financière, à l’instar de l’investissement traditionnel, et la performance extra-financière basée sur la prise en compte des aspects Environnementaux, Sociaux et de la Gouvernance (ESG). Les apports théoriques ainsi que les études empiriques antérieures ont montré une absence d’un consensus évident autour de la performance de l’ISR. Si certains auteurs soutiennent sa surperformance, d’autres insistent sur sa sous performance. De même, certains d’autres déclarent qu’il n’est ni sous ni surperformant, c’est-à-dire qu’il est neutre. Le présent travail de recherche a pour objet d’analyser la performance de l’ISR dans le contexte marocain. En particulier, d’étudier la performance de l’indice le Casablanca ESG10 en comparaison avec celle de l’indice MASI et de l’indice MSI20 (MADEX). D’après les résultats, le Casablanca ESG10 sous performe ses homologues conventionnels en terme du rendement absolu et du rendement ajusté au risque. Les résultats obtenus n’ont aucune significativité statistique. Mots clés : Investissement socialement responsable, Responsabilité sociétale de l’entreprise, critères ESG, performance financière, performance extra-financière. ABSTRACT: Socially Responsible Investment (SRI) is considered the most dominant form of sustainable finance. It is the reflection of CSR within the financial markets. Indeed, this type of investment aims to reconcile financial performance (FP), like traditional investment, and extra-financial performance based on the consideration of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) aspects. Theoretical contributions as well as previous empirical studies have shown a lack of clear consensus around SRI performance. While there are some who support its outperformance, there are also others who insist on its underperformance. Similarly, some others state that it is neither under-nor over-performing, in other words that is neutral. The purpose of this research is to analyze the performance of SRI in the Moroccan context. In particular, to study the performance of the Casablanca ESG10 index in comparison with MASI index and MSI20 (MADEX) index. According to the results, the Casablanca ESG10 underperforms its conventional counterparts in terms of absolute return and risk-adjusted return. The results obtained have no statistical significance. Key words: Socially Responsible Investment, Corporate Social Responsibility, ESG criteria, financial.

title: Mapping highly cited research in FT50 journals: a bibliometric and science-mapping analysis
summary: Purpose The Financial Times 50 (FT50) journal list is a prestigious and influential ranking, widely regarded as a benchmark of excellence in business and economics research. The purpose of the present study was to identify trends and examine the 50 most-cited bibliometric analyses to gain insights into influential publications in management and economics. Design/methodology/approach The Scopus database was used to comprehensively identify the most-cited documents in FT50 journals without year or language restriction. The 50 most-cited publications were retrieved from each of the 50 journals included in the 2016 FT50 list, yielding a corpus of 2,500 publications, which were downloaded in CSV format. Documents were evaluated for various characteristics, including year of publication, document type, names of authors, topic, open access and affiliations. Findings The results found that the MIS Quarterly: Management Information Systems has received the highest citations. Trailblazing researchers such as Shleifer A., Mackenzie S.B. and Podsakoff PM exhibit high citation strength and centrality in co-authorship networks. The study also reveals that University of California was the most productive institution, majority of the institutions were from the USA. Major topics of interest in the top 50 most-cited papers were corporate governance, supply chain management, earnings management and entrepreneurship. Originality/value The study covers to understanding the impact of researchers of FT50 authors and offers insights for academics, organizations and policymakers aiming into the evolution of high-impact business research.

title: Industry 4.0 adoption for supply chain performance in Tunisian companies
summary: Goal: This study aims to investigate the direct and indirect effects of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) on supply chain performance (SCP) in Tunisian firms, by testing the mediating role of supply chain resilience (SCRes) and the moderating role of supply chain visibility (SCV). Design/Methodology/Approach: The analysis collected data from 81 Tunisian companies across diverse sectors, including manufacturing, agri-food, pharmaceutical, and other activities using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the theoretical hypotheses. Smart PLS 4.0 is the statistical software used in this survey. Results: Supply chain resilience significantly mediates this relationship, indicating that I4.0’s full performance benefits are contingent upon strengthening resilience capabilities. Additionally, supply chain visibility positively moderates the link between I4.0 and resilience, demonstrating that higher visibility amplifies the positive effect of I4.0 on SCRes. These findings emphasize that I4.0 generates maximum impact only when combined with resilience and visibility efforts. Limitations of the investigation: This study has five main limitations (cross-sectional design, moderate sample size, self-reported measures, focus on only three I4.0 technologies, and single-country context), which future research should address through longitudinal designs, larger samples, objective data, and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications: This research offers an actionable plan for Tunisia's industrial evolution, showing how a strategic focus on I4.0 -driven resilience and visibility can directly boost the private sector's competitiveness, strengthen the national economy, and ensure a more prosperous position in the global market. Originality/Value: This study extends Qader et al. (2022) by providing the first empirical examination of their integrated I4.0, resilience, visibility, and performance framework in an African emerging economy (Tunisia). While the conceptual model and hypotheses are adapted from Qader et al. (2022), we contribute by validating the framework in a context characterized by fragmented logistics, small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) dominance, and high information asymmetry, conditions that may amplify the importance of visibility mechanisms. The findings offer context-specific insights for other emerging economies.

title: The Role of Green Accounting in Enhancing Corporate Value and Sustainable Economic Performance
summary: Growing environmental pressure has made conventional accounting insufficient, because it often hides environmental costs and leaves managers and investors with an incomplete view of firm performance. This study examines the role of green accounting in enhancing corporate value and sustainable economic performance. Using a qualitative integrative literature review, the study synthesizes theoretical and empirical evidence from reputable academic databases and regulatory publications, analyzed through thematic synthesis. The findings show that green accounting improves cost visibility and resource efficiency, that credible disclosure reduces information asymmetry and raises corporate value, and that long-term economic performance emerges through efficiency, innovation, and risk reduction. These benefits are conditional on disclosure credibility, governance, and institutional pressure, since symbolic reporting may weaken the effect. The study concludes that green accounting is most effective when integrated into internal decision making rather than treated as disclosure alone, and it also offers implications for managers, investors, and Indonesian regulators.

title: Financial reporting quality, corporate law compliance, and shareholder value: Evidence from Saudi joint-stock firms
summary: The subject of discussion in this research paper is the effect of reporting quality on shareholder value in Saudi joint stock companies. Though there are some international papers on the influence of audit oversight and international financial reporting standards (IFRS) on reporting quality, there is a scarcity of empirical studies on the topic among Saudi joint stock companies (Doan et al., 2026; Osemy, 2025). It should be noted that financial statements are developed with the interests of shareholders, the key users of accounting information, in mind (Alshammari, 2025; Al Sharif, 2026; Lampiris et al., 2025; Tran & Dang, 2026). Data were collected via structured questionnaires from 504 people. Then, these data were analyzed using techniques such as descriptive statistics, t-tests, and simple linear regression. Good-quality financial reporting has a positive influence on decision-making of the shareholders, increases their confidence, and allows maximizing their profit. Simple linear regression analysis reveals that there is a significant positive correlation between the two variables under consideration. The findings of the study are consistent with Vision 2030, as they increase financial transparency and corporate governance in Saudi capital markets. Concerning this issue, Doan et al. (2026) and Osemy (2025) point to the absence of empirical studies among Saudi joint stock companies on the influence of IFRS and audit oversight. Furthermore, Alshammari (2025), Al Sharif (2026), Lampiris et al. (2025), and Tran and Dang (2026) confirm that financial statements serve the interests of shareholders, the key users of accounting information.

title: CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY AND TAX AVOIDANCE REGULATION: A TWO-WAY INTERPLAY
summary: Abstract Corporate social responsibility, increasingly framed through environmental, social and governance practices, remains under-integrated within corporate taxation. This article analyses the two-way interplay between responsibility norms and the legal regulation of tax avoidance. It argues that responsibility is neither wholly extra-legal nor purely voluntary, while tax law alone is constrained by definitional indeterminacy, limits of legal design and enforcement, structural arbitrage opportunities, business lobbying and weaknesses in public accountability. Responsibility norms can strengthen tax governance and transparency; legal rules can, in turn, discipline responsibility initiatives through disclosure and accountability. Their interaction provides a more credible framework for constraining aggressive avoidance and strengthening corporate accountability in taxation.

title: Geopolitical Risk and Equity Markets: Supply-Chain Exposure and Stock-Market Reactions to the 2019 US–China Tariffs
summary: Abstract Geopolitical developments, including trade restrictions and tariffs, can disrupt international supply chains and influence financial markets. However, companies may experience different stock-market reactions depending on their exposure to affected countries and suppliers. This study investigates the extent to which supply-chain exposure predicts stock-market reactions among publicly listed textile and apparel companies following the 2019 increase in United States tariffs on Chinese imports. Historical share-price data, market-index returns, and corporate disclosures will be collected to measure companies' financial performance and dependence on affected supply chains. An event-study methodology will be used to calculate abnormal returns and cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) around the selected event. A cross-sectional regression will then examine the relationship between supply-chain exposure and CAR, controlling for relevant company characteristics where data permit. The study aims to assess whether differences in supply-chain exposure help explain variations in stock-market reactions to geopolitical trade actions. Its findings may contribute to understanding how international supply-chain structures influence firms' financial vulnerability. However, the analysis will recognise limitations arising from incomplete corporate disclosures, anticipated policy changes, and other market developments occurring around the event.

title: Corporate Governance in India
summary: Corporate Governance is the system of processes, principles, and policies through which a company is directed and controlled, and its failure can bring down even profitable companies. This article explains why investor protection a legal concern is as well as a financial one. It examines how the Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015 give legal force to the principles of accountability and transparency. Using the collapse of IL&FS and the Satyam scandal as case studies, it shows how weak board oversight, ineffective audit committees and inadequate internal controls allow financial misreporting to go undetected, and it traces the regulatory response that followed Satyam. This article argues that India has considerably strengthened its legal framework, but that corporate governance ultimately depends on accountability in practice and not merely in rule.

title: Technologically driven corporate sustainability: hospitality and tourism and fintech
summary: Purpose This article aims to reveal the impact, mechanism of action and boundary conditions (heterogeneity) of fintech on the environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance of listed hotel and tourism enterprises in China, thereby constructing a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between the two and enriching and expanding the theory of sustainable development of enterprises. Design/methodology/approach We select 148 Chinese-listed hospitality and tourism as the research sample, empirically examine the role of fintech on the ESG performance of these firms and explore their potential influence mechanisms. Findings This study finds that fintech significantly enhances firm ESG performance. Moreover, fintech improves ESG performance of firms through financing constraints and external monitoring, while business risk mitigates the positive effects of fintech on firm ESG performance. The heterogeneity analysis indicates that the positive effect of fintech is more pronounced for regions with lower economic policy uncertainty and lower environmental regulation, as well as firms with high digitization and nonstate ownership. Research limitations/implications Firstly, there are deficiencies in the measurement of fintech. Future research will employ big data, text mining and machine learning technologies to develop more accurate fintech measurement indicators and mitigate endogenous issues such as measurement errors. Secondly, this article delves into the purview of fintech in influencing the H.T. firms' ESG performance from financing constraints, external supervision and business risks. Future research will utilize multidisciplinary cross-fertilization methods to further explore how fintech influences ESG performance. Thirdly, the current ESG disclosure of Chinese-listed firms is voluntary, and the conclusions drawn from this may have some limitations. Originality/value With the rapid advancement of fintech, H.T. firms have increasingly recognized its importance in addressing challenges related to difficult and costly financing. Nonetheless, the existing literature reveals substantial gaps in understanding how fintech influences H.T. firms' ESG performance, particularly due to the absence of a unified framework for systematically examining underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions. Accordingly, this study seeks to develop a multi-level explanatory framework that integrates information asymmetry theory, financing constraint theory, reputation theory and resource dependence theory. This framework enables a more comprehensive understanding of the transmission mechanisms and boundary conditions through which fintech influences ESG performance in H.T. firms, while providing a rational explanation of how fintech can optimize investment decision-making within these enterprises.

title: Is It Time to Change the Climate for ESG Investing?
summary: Individual investors have been intrigued by the possibility of merging their personal values with their investing goals for some time. Institutional investors are also increasingly open to considering environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors when making investment decisions. Prior studies on ESG investing have focused on corporate financial performance, the presence of alpha, and risk mitigation. This study focuses on future stock returns over long-term time horizons. We find largely negative relationships among ESG scores and future stock returns. The analysis also explores returns to alternative combinations of ESG subcomponents (e.g., ES, SG, and EG). The tests of these subcomponent score combinations also reveal negative future return relationships. The results of this and other similar studies are highly dependent on the ESG score database that is used.

title: Firm’s financial flexibility, corporate governance, and investment efficiency: The evidence from an emerging country
summary: Using data from Vietnamese non-financial listed companies between 2010 and 2024, this study investigates the determinants of investment efficiency, specifically focusing on the dual problems of overinvestment and underinvestment. To achieve these research objectives, the study employs the System Generalised Method of Moments (SGMM) estimation technique to analyse the data and obtain robust empirical results. First, our empirical findings reveal that higher financial flexibility provides firms with readily available internal funds. However, these abundant financial resources tend to weaken external monitoring and increase managerial discretion, thereby fostering overinvestment. Similarly, state ownership exhibits a positive and significant relationship with investment inefficiency. This aligns with the soft-budget-constraints theory, where anticipated state backing dilutes financial discipline and drives overinvestment. Conversely, firm size is negatively correlated with investment inefficiency, indicating that the superior monitoring and governance inherent in larger firms effectively restrain managerial discretion. At the macro level, economic booms and loosened lending standards further amplify free cash flow problems and soften firms’ budget constraints, thereby exacerbating investment inefficiency. Ultimately, the findings of this study provide policymakers and managers with actionable recommendations to strengthen the Vietnamese corporate finance landscape and promote greater investment efficiency.

title: Structural dependency and environmental challenges in the Indonesia–China nickel supply chain for electric vehicle production
summary: This study investigates the Indonesia–China nickel supply chain in electric vehicle (EV) production through the framework of dependency theory, focusing on its structural economic and environmental impacts. Despite Indonesia’s position as the world’s largest nickel producer and China’s dominance in EV manufacturing and battery production, the bilateral cooperation reveals a dependency pattern marked by Chinese control over Indonesia’s nickel refining sector, Indonesia’s balance of payments deficits worsened by profit repatriation, and technological monopolies upheld by Chinese investments. This dependency structurally limits Indonesia’s capacity for sustainable development and environmental governance. The resulting environmental consequences include deforestation, air and water pollution, driven by weak regulatory enforcement and prioritization of foreign investment interests. The study employs a qualitative descriptive method using secondary data sources and triangulation for validity. It applies Dos Santos’ New Dependency framework to analyze economic and technological asymmetries. The findings highlight that Indonesia’s nickel sector growth, while economically beneficial, perpetuates ecological harm as an inherent outcome of dependency.

title: CSR Reporting as Strategic Communication: Financial Reporting Quality and Its Stakeholder Communication Implications
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Financial Reporting Quality (FRQ) and explores the communication implications of reporting quality improvements. A sequential explanatory mixed‐methods design was employed. In the first stage, survey data from 150 finance professionals employed by London Stock Exchange (LSE)‐listed companies were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS‐SEM). In the second stage, a qualitative content analysis of reports and disclosures from 32 LSE‐listed firms was conducted through the lens of Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) Theory. The findings indicate that CSR is positively and significantly associated with relevance, faithful representation, understandability, and comparability. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: transparency signals, simplification of information, comparative advantage communication, consistency across platforms, and stakeholder‐centric narratives. These themes illustrate how reporting quality may support communication credibility, message clarity and consistency, stakeholder‐oriented communication, and organizational positioning, while such communication outcomes are interpreted as exploratory implications rather than directly measured effects. The study contributes by positioning financial reporting quality as a communication‐enabling mechanism linking CSR initiatives with stakeholder communication processes and by introducing comparative advantage communication as an interpretive insight emerging from the qualitative findings. The findings offer implications for managers, reporting professionals, and policymakers seeking to enhance transparency, reporting quality, and stakeholder communication.

title: Predicting supply chain bottlenecks with real-time data: a bibliometric review of transport and logistics research from 2016 to 2025
summary: Abstract Supply chain bottlenecks are critical constraints that disrupt the smooth flow of goods, often triggering delays that cascade through interconnected processes and weaken overall resilience. In an era of digital transformation, the ability to anticipate such constraints through real-time data and predictive analytics has become increasingly important, yet the existing literature remains fragmented across transportation, logistics, and information systems, leaving conceptual boundaries blurred and practical insights underdeveloped. Addressing this gap, we conducted a bibliometric review of 3638 Scopus-indexed publications from 2016 to 2025, using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to analyse publication patterns, keyword clusters, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a strong concentration in intelligent transportation systems, with traffic congestion emerging as the most frequent theme, and four clusters identified around traffic management and detection, congestion and travel-time modelling, data infrastructure and analytics, and short-horizon flow control. A clear shift is observed between 2016–2020 and 2021–2025, marked by the growing prominence of machine learning and deep learning approaches. The study contributes by distinguishing transport-level prediction from supply chain-level bottleneck management. It further proposes a research agenda that emphasises cross-context validation, prediction-to-action integration, and explicit tests of forecast usefulness, thereby offering both theoretical clarity and practical guidance for strengthening supply chain performance.

title: When Climate Policies Overlap: The Effect of Stacked Urban Climate Pilot Programs on Manufacturing Firms’ Supply Chain Resilience in China
summary: Can the simultaneous deployment of two urban climate programs strengthen a manufacturer’s supply chain resilience (SCR), and does the order in which the programs are introduced matter? China’s climate-adaptive city construction (CACC) pilot, launched in 2017, overlapped in nine prefecture-level cities with the sponge city construction pilot (SCP), which had been rolled out in two batches in 2015 and 2016. This staggered overlap provides a quasi-experiment that distinguishes a stacked climate policy treatment from either program operating alone. Using a balanced panel of 552 Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2010 to 2024 and a two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences design, this study documents that firms in cities designated under both programs exhibit significantly higher SCR after 2017 than firms in non-overlap cities, and that this difference shows no obvious pre-trend and cannot be reproduced by placebo reassignment. The preferred specification implies an increase of 0.067, equivalent to about 18.7% of the sample mean SCR. The stacked treatment is associated with three firm-level responses that track SCR, namely a higher share of green patents, greater productive risk-taking, and stronger environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. The effect is concentrated in the southeast of the Hu Huanyong Line, in non-state-owned enterprises, and in firms where the board chair also serves as chief executive officer. Further analysis shows that the CACC program alone does not significantly raise SCR, whereas the SCP program does; combining the two produces a larger effect than either single program, and the synergy arises mainly when climate-adaptation measures are added to a city that has already built a sponge city foundation. The findings suggest that urban climate policy should be coordinated across programs and sequenced to exploit institutional complementarities rather than evaluated program by program.

title: ESG media buzz and firm performance: the moderating effect of firms’ strategic emphasis
summary: While firms increasingly invest in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) initiatives, stakeholders’ awareness of these efforts depends largely on external communication. Prior research focuses on the performance implications of ESG practices themselves, overlooking the role of ESG-related media visibility. This study examines how ESG media buzz links to firm value and risk. Analysing publicly listed US food and beverage firms, the results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between ESG media buzz and firm value, which weakens when firms strategically prioritise value appropriation over value creation. Additionally, ESG media buzz exhibits a U-shaped relationship with firm risk. These findings highlight the strategic importance of understanding externally mediated ESG visibility and its interpretation in capital markets.

title: PRIVATE OPERATOR MANAGEMENT, CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND VISITOR SATISFACTION IN CAVE TOURISM: A PARALLEL-MEDIATION ANALYSIS OF THE OXALIS PORTFOLIO IN VIETNAM
summary: While private operators increasingly manage ecologically sensitive protected areas, how their management practices relate to visitor satisfaction remains underexplored in cave-tourism research. This study examines a dual parallel mediation model in which Private Operator Management is associated with Visitor Satisfaction, both directly and indirectly through Environmental Conservation Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Visitor Environmental Awareness. Data were collected via a 30-item online questionnaire from 317 visitors across seven cave-tour formats operated by Oxalis Adventure Tours in Phong Nha- Kẻ Bàng National Park and Tú Làn, Vietnam, in the 2024-2025 season. SPSS-based analysis validated the measurement model via confirmatory factor analysis and assessed mediation using bootstrapped confidence intervals (5,000 iterations; Hayes, 2018), with the Baron and Kenny (1986) steps retained as a comparability baseline. The model explains 83.2% of the variance in satisfaction; both indirect effects are significant, accounting for 25.9% (CSR) and 22.8% (awareness) of the total effect. An exploratory subgroup analysis is consistent with a crossover: first-time visitors weight the awareness pathway, repeat visitors the CSR pathway. Common-method-variance and discriminant-validity limitations are discussed.

title: Integrating Internet of Things and Blockchain Technology in Accounting Information Systems: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for Accounting Information Quality
summary: The swift advancement of digital technology has generated novel prospects for enhancing the efficiency of Accounting Information Systems (AIS). Among these innovations, the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain has significant capacity to revolutionize the gathering, processing, validation, and dissemination of accounting data. The Internet of Things facilitates the automatic and real-time collection of operational data through interconnected devices and sensors, whereas blockchain offers a communal, immutable ledger of transactions that enhances traceability and accountability. Incorporating these technologies could enhance the promptness, dependability, clarity, and verifiability of financial data. This study explores the prospective amalgamation of IoT and blockchain in Accounting Information Systems, concentrating on inventory accounting, fixed-asset oversight, transaction validation, financial reporting, and ongoing auditing. It employs a theoretical research methodology grounded in an examination of pertinent scholarly literature. The document also highlights significant obstacles to adoption, including as cybersecurity threats, data privacy issues, costs of implementation, interoperability, regulatory obligations, and the dependability of information gathered from physical devices. The article suggests a cohesive structure where IoT devices document operational occurrences, blockchain maintains authenticated transaction records, and the AIS compiles accounting entries and produces financial statements. The research determines that the integration of IoT and blockchain could enhance the quality of accounting information, contingent upon the implementation of suitable internal controls, governance structures, and expert supervision.

title: THE ROLE OF REGULATORY INSTITUTIONS IN PROMOTING EFFECTIVE CORPORATE GOVERNANCE IN UGANDA: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE
summary: Corporate governance failures have repeatedly shaped Uganda's financial and public sectors, yet scholarly and professional evidence on how regulatory institutions promote effective governance is scattered across disciplines and source types. This paper reports a systematic literature review, structured around the PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, of 18 sources identified through structured searches of open scholarly, repository, regulatory, professional and law-reporting sources in October 2026. A thematic synthesis, informed by agency theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory and responsive regulation, yields five findings. First, Uganda's governance architecture is sector-fragmented, combining statutory regulators, line ministries, audit and anti-corruption bodies and a voluntary professional institute without enforcement powers. Second, the most rigorous evidence indicates that codification has outpaced enforcement, with corruption and weak underlying frameworks limiting the effect of codes. Third, reform has been reactive, recurring after bank failures and most recently through the Financial Institutions (Corporate Governance) Regulations 2024. Fourth, evidence on state-owned enterprises is dominated by unpublished case studies reporting weak boards and accountability gaps. Fifth, litigation arising from the Crane Bank takeover shows that regulators' own powers are bounded by statutory procedure and judicial oversight. The review identifies gaps, chiefly the absence of peer-reviewed evaluations of enforcement outcomes, and sets out implications for research, policy and practice. Because the evidence base was assembled from open sources rather than subscription databases, the findings should be treated as a structured, transparent synthesis and not an exhaustive census.

title: SMART BUILDINGS AND ESG COMPLIANCE: A CASE STUDY OF CHINESE HIGH-RISE DEVELOPMENTS
summary: China's green building sector has become the world's largest, with the Chinese mainland ranking first globally in LEED certifications for the ninth consecutive year and its smart building market projected to more than double from $96.3 billion in 2025 to $206.4 billion by 2031. This article examines how smart building technologies support Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) compliance in Chinese high-rise developments, using Shanghai Tower as an illustrative case. The analysis finds that environmental gains from smart systems are well documented and substantial, with reported energy and water savings of 15–50% depending on intervention type, while social and governance dimensions remain comparatively underdeveloped, constrained by a “triple institutional dilemma” of carbon lock-in, human-capital alienation, and ambiguous governance structures in China's construction sector. The article concludes that smart building technology is necessary but not sufficient for full ESG compliance, and that governance frameworks — not sensors — are the binding constraint on China's high-rise sustainability transition.

title: The Impact of Green Accounting and Corporate Social Responsibility Implementation on Company Values
summary: This study is entitled The Effect of Green Accounting Implementation and Corporate Social Responsibility on Firm Value. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the role of green accounting implementation and corporate social responsibility disclosure in influencing firm value in energy sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2022-2024 period. The research problem focuses on whether these two variables have a significant effect on firm value. This study employs a quantitative approach using secondary data obtained from annual reports and sustainability reports. The sample was selected using the purposive sampling method, resulting in 11 companies with a total of 33 observation units. Data processing and analysis were conducted using panel data regression with the assistance of the EViews application. The results indicate that the implementation of green accounting has a positive and significant effect on firm value, reflecting that transparency related to environmental costs and activities can enhance investor confidence. In contrast, corporate social responsibility shows a negative and significant effect on firm value, suggesting that CSR disclosure has not yet been fully perceived as providing direct economic benefits by investors in the energy sector. This study is expected to contribute to the development of environmental accounting literature and serve as a reference for companies and investors in decision-making processes.

title: The Mechanism of Digital Economy Development on Energy Intensity under the “Dual Carbon” Goals
summary: Reducing energy intensity has became important in the context of the “dual carbon” goals. Panel data were collected from 30 provinces in China during the period of 2011-2020 to investigate how the digital economy affects energy intensity and the mechanisms underlies. The empirical findings indicate that digital economy development significantly lowers energy intensity. A series of robustness checks confirm that this result is not coincidental. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the energy-reduction effect is more pronounced in non-resource-based provinces and the western region, while varying degrees of heterogeneity are observed in resource‑based provinces and the eastern and central regions. This paper elucidates the intrinsic mechanisms through which the digital economy enhances energy efficiency at the provincial level, providing empirical support and practical insights for promoting coordinated development of digitalization and greening under the “dual carbon” goals, as well as for formulating region‑specific energy transition policies.

title: Systemic Greenwashing in Sustainable Finance: How EU Regulations Launder Carbon-Intensive Assets Into Sustainable Investments
summary: This article introduces the concept of systemic greenwashing. Drawing on original empirical analysis of “green” investment funds with the European Union’s highest sustainability classification, it addresses the striking paradox that portfolios classified by EU regulations as “green” are drastically more carbon intensive than those with no sustainability objectives, despite no evidence of falsified disclosures. Combining close analysis of EU regulations with detailed case studies of corporations that dominate “green” portfolios, the article demonstrates that greenwashing in this context is not the result of corporate deception or weak enforcement, but is instead performed by regulatory processes which reclassify carbon-intensive corporate activities into sustainable contributions to decarbonisation. The implications for criminology are significant, reframing greenwashing as a structural form of state-corporate harm.

title: Sustainable Supply Chain Management Practices and Performance of Food and Beverage Manufacturing Firms in Nairobi City County, Kenya.
summary: The food and beverage manufacturing sector operates in an increasingly uncertain supply chain environment characterized by resource scarcity, environmental degradation, rising regulatory pressure and growing consumer demand for environmentally responsible products. Sustainable supply chain management has emerged as an important approach through which firms can reduce environmental risk while achieving profitability and market share objectives. However, the uptake of sustainable practices among food and beverage manufacturers in Kenya remains inconsistent, and many firms are yet to realize the full performance benefits of these practices. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to establish the influence of sustainable supply chain management practices on the performance of food and beverage manufacturing firms in Nairobi City County, Kenya. It examined four practices, namely sustainable sourcing, reverse logistics, eco-innovation and sustainable packaging. The study was anchored on the Resource Dependence Theory, Systems Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Circular Economy Theory. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted, targeting 95 food and beverage manufacturing firms in Nairobi City County listed by the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, with supply chain managers and procurement officers as the units of observation. A sample of 128 respondents was determined using the Yamane formula and selected through stratified random sampling. Primary data were collected using a self-administered structured questionnaire, which was pilot tested on 12 respondents; all Cronbach’s alpha coefficients exceeded 0.70. Data were analysed using SPSS version 28 through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis. A total of 110 questionnaires were returned, a response rate of 85.9%. The findings revealed that the four practices jointly explained 52.1% of the variation in performance. Eco-innovation had the strongest influence on performance, followed by sustainable sourcing, reverse logistics and sustainable packaging, all of which were positive and statistically significant. The study concluded that sustainable supply chain management practices are significant drivers of the performance of food and beverage manufacturing firms. The study therefore recommends that firms should prioritize organically or sustainably certified inputs and maintain supplier sustainability performance databases; streamline returns processes and integrate recycling programmes into supply chain operations; align ecological product design with consumer demand; and strengthen reusable packaging return systems, recycling labels and supplier monitoring for non-hazardous packaging materials.

title: It is all about digitalization: investigating antecedents and effects of digital transformation
summary: Abstract Digital transformation is increasingly recognized as a vital driver of competitiveness, yet the precise organizational factors that most strongly influence its success remain ambiguous. This study addresses this gap by examining how strategic, operational, organizational, and cultural factors jointly relate to digital transformation outcomes, and by uncovering the mediating role of innovation success in shaping overall company success. Drawing upon data from 279 organizational key informants in Germany with substantive involvement in digital transformation, this study develops a holistic framework that not only identifies key organizational factors relevant for digital transformation success but also compares their associations with transformation success when considered simultaneously. The findings reveal numerically larger associations for cultural and operational factors, whereas strategic and organizational factors exhibit smaller coefficients, with the organizational-domain association only marginally significant ( p < 0.10). Although bootstrap-based parameter-difference tests do not support a statistically established ranking of the four domains, the results underline the relevance of all four domains while suggesting that cultural and operational conditions may warrant particular attention depending on firms’ specific transformation context. Furthermore, the results reveal a significant indirect association between digital transformation success and company success through innovation success, accounting for around 60% of the total association in the specified model. Hence, organizations seeking to maximize the returns on their digital initiatives should consider cultural and operational conditions alongside the strategic and organizational foundations of digital transformation. Taken together, these insights offer actionable guidance for businesses aiming to allocate their resources strategically, consider cultural and operational conditions as important diagnostic starting points, and harness the full potential of digital transformation through a concerted emphasis on innovation.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN RAIL FREIGHT: LEVERAGING IOT AND BLOCKCHAIN FOR OPTIMIZING THE CHINA-EUROPE EXPRESS RAILWAY
summary: The China-Europe Express Railway has grown into a corridor carrying more than three million TEUs annually, yet its continued efficiency gains increasingly depend on digital rather than physical infrastructure. This article examines how the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain are being applied to optimize the corridor's cargo visibility, customs clearance, and documentation processes. Drawing on recent industry and academic literature, the study finds that IoT applications — from satellite-based container tracking to wagon-condition sensors — are already deployed at meaningful scale, while blockchain applications remain comparatively nascent, concentrated in customs and trade-documentation pilots. The two technologies are shown to be complementary rather than substitutable: IoT generates the real-time operational data that blockchain-based systems require to create trustworthy, shared, and auditable records among the corridor's many independent railway administrations, customs authorities, and freight forwarders. The analysis concludes that sequencing IoT investment ahead of blockchain deployment is the more pragmatic near-term pathway.

title: Responsabilité sociétale des entreprises et performance globale : une revue de littérature conceptuelle à la lumière du marketing responsable
summary: Résumé : La responsabilité sociétale des entreprises (RSE) occupe aujourd'hui une place centrale dans les débats académiques et managériaux relatifs à la gouvernance, à la durabilité et à la performance des organisations. Si la littérature établit une association globalement positive entre RSE et performance, elle demeure fragmentée quant aux mécanismes qui expliquent cette relation : les cadres relationnels de la RSE (parties prenantes, légitimité) et les travaux consacrés à la communication responsable restent rarement articulés, et le rôle médiateur du marketing responsable demeure insuffisamment théorisé, notamment dans les économies émergentes. C'est précisément cette lacune que le présent article se propose de combler. Sur la base d'une revue de littérature narrative et conceptuelle couvrant la période 1953-2025 et mobilisant les bases de données Scopus, Web of Science et Google Scholar selon des critères explicites de pertinence et de qualité scientifique, l'article analyse les principales approches théoriques de la RSE, son évolution vers une logique stratégique, ses liens avec la performance globale et les mécanismes susceptibles d'expliquer cette relation. L'analyse met en évidence le rôle central de la théorie des parties prenantes, de la théorie de la légitimité, de la Resource-Based View, de la théorie institutionnelle et des capacités dynamiques, tout en discutant leurs tensions et leurs complémentarités. Elle montre que le marketing responsable peut constituer un mécanisme de traduction stratégique permettant de transformer les engagements RSE en valeur perçue, en confiance, en légitimité et en performance globale, sous réserve de crédibilité et de cohérence, le greenwashing constituant le principal facteur de fragilisation de ce processus. La contribution originale de l'article, qui le distingue des synthèses antérieures sur le lien RSE-performance, réside dans un modèle conceptuel intégrateur plaçant le marketing responsable en position de variable médiatrice, assorti de six propositions de recherche opérationnalisées et de conditions frontières explicites, applicables au contexte marocain et particulièrement aux entreprises labellisées RSE par la CGEM. Mots clés : RSE ; performance globale ; marketing responsable ; parties prenantes ; légitimité ; développement durable ; gouvernance. JEL Classification : M14 ; M31 ; Q56 Type du papier : Recherche Théorique. Abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has become a central issue in academic and managerial debates on governance, sustainability and organizational performance. Although the literature establishes an overall positive association between CSR and performance, it remains fragmented as to the mechanisms explaining this relationship: the relational frameworks of CSR (stakeholders, legitimacy) and the research devoted to responsible communication are rarely articulated, and the mediating role of responsible marketing remains insufficiently theorized, particularly in emerging economies. This is precisely the gap that the present article aims to fill. Based on a narrative and conceptual literature review covering the period 1953-2025 and drawing on the Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases according to explicit relevance and scientific quality criteria, the article analyzes the main theoretical approaches to CSR, its evolution toward a strategic logic, its relationship with global performance and the mechanisms that may explain this relationship. The analysis highlights the central role of stakeholder theory, legitimacy theory, the Resource-Based View, institutional theory and dynamic capabilities, while discussing their tensions and complementarities. It shows that responsible marketing can act as a strategic translation mechanism through which CSR commitments are transformed into perceived value, trust, legitimacy and global performance, provided that credibility and consistency are ensured, greenwashing being the main factor weakening this process. The original contribution of the article, which distinguishes it from previous syntheses on the CSR-performance link, lies in an integrative conceptual model positioning responsible marketing as a mediating variable, together with six operationalized research propositions and explicit boundary conditions, applicable to the Moroccan context and particularly to companies awarded the CGEM CSR Label. Keywords: CSR; global performance; responsible marketing; stakeholders; legitimacy; sustainability; governance. Classification JEL: M14; M31; Q56 Paper type: Theoretical Research.

title: Substance versus symbolism: how ESG dimensions relate to financial performance in family firms
summary: Purpose This study examines how ESG performance, environmental innovation, exposure to ESG controversies, and internal governance mechanisms are associated with the financial performance of listed family firms. Socioemotional wealth (SEW) is used as an interpretive lens rather than measured as a moderator. Design/methodology/approach A near-balanced panel of 83 firms from the Global 500 Family Business Index over 2016–2023 (662 firm-year observations) is analysed using two-way fixed effects models with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. Robustness checks include clustered and bootstrap inference, lagged specifications and an alternative measure of controversy. Regional differences are examined in an exploratory pooled interaction model. Findings ESG performance is positively associated with Tobin's Q but not with accounting metrics. Environmental innovation is associated with higher ROE, although this association does not survive conservative inference. Controversy exposure is associated with lower ROA and ROE. The only result robust to every inference procedure concerns governance: where boards reach a critical mass of female directors, the market valuation of ESG is reversed rather than amplified. Practical implications ESG score optimisation should not be treated as a route to accounting value in family firms. Boards should not assume that formal gender diversity reinforces the credibility of ESG commitments. Originality/value The study integrates ESG performance, environmental innovation, controversy exposure, and board governance into a single framework for large family firms and shows that board composition operates as a boundary condition of the ESG market signal.

title: A Conceptual Model for Enhancing Sustainable Performance: The Synergy Of Green Innovation Based on Green Skills and Green Creative Self-Efficacy in Metalcraft MSMES
summary: Metalcraft micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Bali contribute to the island’s craft economy, yet their transition to environmentally responsible production may be constrained by limited technical resources and uneven environmental capabilities. Although recent MSME studies associate green innovation with business performance, findings concerning environmental performance remain mixed, and previous studies rarely examine owners’ green skills and green creative self-efficacy together in traditional metalcraft enterprises. This study tests the effects of Green Skill and Green Creative Self-Efficacy on Sustainable Performance, with Green Innovation as a mediator, and identifies managerial priorities through Importance-Performance Map Analysis (IPMA). Survey data were obtained from 259 owners of metalcraft MSMEs in Bali Province using proportionate stratified random sampling and analyzed with PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4. The estimated relationships are positive and statistically significant, and Green Innovation partially mediates the relationships between both capability constructs and Sustainable Performance. Green Creative Self-Efficacy has numerically larger path coefficients than Green Skill for Green Innovation and Sustainable Performance; this coefficient ordering is interpreted descriptively because a formal between-coefficient difference test was not reported. IPMA identifies environmental awareness and pollution-control facility deployment as specific improvement priorities. The study extends MSME sustainability research by linking an individual-level cognitive capability with operational innovation in a traditional craft setting. For practice, the results support combining practical green-skills training with confidence-building problem-solving activities and affordable, context-appropriate pollution-control and waste-management measures.

title: ESG Performance and Financial Outcomes in the Hospitality Industry: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: ABSTRACT Corporate social responsibility (CSR) and ESG are in the spotlight in hospitality management research; however, the CSR/ESG body of knowledge is fragmented by incompatible measurement approaches. Most of this work has been conducted at the regional level, with little to no attention to governance issues. To date, no study has combined a systematic review of the CSR/ESG literature in the hospitality industry with a pre‐registered design incorporating bibliometric analysis and a meta‐analytic approach. The main objectives are to map the research landscape on ESG/CSR to financial performance linkages for the hospitality industry (RQ1), to evaluate the combined strength of association and the direction of the ESG‐to‐performance linkage along with the structural moderators of this relationship through a meta‐analytic approach (RQ2), and to integrate the primary mediation processes, moderation variables, and research gaps, particularly about the governance dimension (RQ3). Peer‐reviewed empirical studies, along with non‐empirical studies, that have examined ESG or CSR as an independent variable and financial performance as a dependent variable for hospitality sector firms (hotels, restaurants, casino hotels, cruise lines, and resort complexes), limiting the language to English and the publication period to 2010 to 2026. We searched the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus on January 12, 2026. We used six parallel search strings to address all three research questions, covering ESG/CSR, hospitality, and financial performance. Sensitivity was 100% because the search retrieved all 12 pre‐identified gold‐standard studies. Results showed a substantial duplication rate (49.6%) between the two databases. The protocol was registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF) before data collection (V5; all amendments were filed before each analytical stage). We assessed the empirical studies using a hybrid of the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale (NOS, max 9) and a custom five‐item Econometric Quality Checklist. Risk‐of‐bias (RoB) inter‐rater reliability ( N = 47 dual‐reviewed studies, 50% verification sample) reached Po = 83.5% and Cohen's κ = 0.791 after resolving discrepancies, satisfying the pre‐registered ≥ 80% Po and ≥ 0.60 κ thresholds. All 47 RoB weight category assignments reached full agreement. Literature review studies were assessed using A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews AMSTAR‐2. Ninety‐five studies included in total (72 empirical, 23 non‐empirical). K = 23 studies ( k = 84 effect sizes) were eligible for meta‐analytic pooling. The primary three‐level multilevel random‐effects model yielded r = 0.211 (95% CI [0.103, 0.314], p = 0.0001; I 2 = 93.3%). The one‐per‐study model yielded r = 0.216 (95% CI [0.106, 0.320], p = 0.0001). Restricting the pool to objective third‐party ESG ratings yielded r = 0.061 ( p = 0.195), while self‐reported CSR surveys yielded r = 0.353 ( p < 0.001). Funnel asymmetry was detected (Egger's test: z = 2.732, p = 0.013), but trim‐and‐fill imputed zero missing studies; PET‐PEESE bias‐corrected estimates are non‐significant, consistent with measurement‐type heterogeneity rather than suppression bias. The governance ESG dimension yielded r = −0.023 from five studies. SciMat longitudinal co‐word analysis confirmed the ESG cluster growing from marginal (centrality = 8.37, P1) to structurally prominent (centrality = 17.71, P4), with the CSR‐to‐ESG terminological transition underway but still incomplete. The positive ESG‐to‐financial‐performance association in the hospitality industry is entirely dependent on measurement: objective third‐party ratings show no detectable association, whereas self‐reported property‐level CSR measures show a large positive effect. This divergence is a structurally diagnostic finding that generates two competing hypotheses: the construct validity hypothesis (enterprise‐level and property‐level ESG instruments target theoretically distinct constructs with different pathways to financial performance) and the methodological account (common method bias inflates self‐reported estimates), which cannot be disentangled because the ESG measurement approach and study design are fully collinear in the pool. The governance dimension is the field's primary intellectual deficit, established convergently across three evidence streams (bibliometric, thematic, researcher self‐report) and consistent with the meta‐analytic arm ( r = −0.023, K = 5), which is too sparse to estimate the relationship reliably and is itself a structural signal of the deficit. The primary value‐creation mechanisms, corporate reputation, competitive advantage, and ESG as organizational insurance during crises, are theoretically coherent but causally underidentified.

title: TSMC, discrimination litigation and sustainability reporting
summary: Research methodology This case was developed using secondary data sources. Primary case materials were drawn from official public filings, specifically TSMC’s annual Form 20-F and sustainability reports, both publicly accessible online. Supplementary context was gathered from news coverage and publicly available media coverage on TSMC’s US operations. Applicable financial reporting standards, specifically International Accounting Standard (IAS) 37, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and industry-specific disclosure standards issued by the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) were also consulted and are included as appendices to the case.Instructor Note on SASB/ISSB Governance: SASB is no longer an independent organization. In August 2022, the Value Reporting Foundation, which housed SASB, was consolidated into the IFRS Foundation, and responsibility for the SASB Standards transferred to the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). The industry-based SASB Standards remain in use and are now maintained by the ISSB. For simplicity and to facilitate students’ reading and research, the terms “SASB” and “SASB Standards” are retained throughout the case and teaching note.The protagonist, Wen-Chang Hao, is a composite character created for teaching purposes. Her title, responsibilities and organizational position are based on the publicly available LinkedIn profile of an individual holding a comparable role within TSMC’s sustainability function, as well as TSMC’s public sustainability disclosures and corporate governance documentation. No individual by this name has been identified as holding this position at TSMC, and the character’s deliberations and decisions are constructed for pedagogical purposes rather than drawn from any primary or firsthand source. Case overview/synopsis Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest semiconductor foundry with over 70% global market share, confronted a disclosure decision as Wen-Chang Hao, Global Sustainability Engagement and Strategy Manager, drafted the company’s 2025 Sustainability Report for its internal May 2026 deadline. Two active US class-action lawsuits had emerged against TSMC’s US operations: one alleging racial and national-origin discrimination involving more than 30 plaintiffs in the Arizona plant, and a second filed in April 2026 alleging systemic gender discrimination potentially affecting thousands of current and former female employees. Neither lawsuit had been identified as a named legal contingency in TSMC’s most recently submitted Form 20-F.Hao’s decision represented a double materiality problem. Financial reporting standards permitted the omission of both lawsuits in the absence of a reliable damage estimate, while TSMC’s voluntary sustainability/ESG frameworks created no binding obligation to disclose. Yet the gap between the two reporting channels, one silent on workforce litigation, the other publicly celebrating global sustainability/ESG leadership, raised substantive questions that Hao had to resolve: whether to acknowledge the pending litigation in the 2025 Sustainability Report, at what level of specificity and in which sections, and how to frame any disclosure relative to the annual report and financial statement’s treatment of the same matters. Complexity academic level This case addresses loss contingency recognition, materiality judgment and ESG disclosure across financial and nonfinancial reporting channels. It is appropriate for upper-level undergraduate and graduate courses, depending on the depth of analysis and instructor emphasis. It is suitable for courses including Intermediate Accounting, Auditing, Sustainability Accounting and Human Resource Management. It may also be used in International Business courses, particularly in discussions of multinational reporting environments and the cross-functional implications of workforce-related challenges and risks. The case is recommended for use mid-to-late in the term, after students have been introduced to either contingent liability standards (in accounting courses) or stakeholder theory and materiality frameworks (in Sustainability/ESG or IB courses).The case was pilot-tested in an undergraduate International Business course with approximately 25 students majoring in accounting, finance or management participating in the discussion. Student engagement and feedback informed subsequent refinements to the case materials and teaching notes.

title: Corporate Governance, ESG Disclosure and Firm Value in an Emerging Market
summary: Purpose: This paper examines how corporate governance and the disclosure of environmental, social and governance (ESG) information have co-evolved in Vietnam between 2015 and 2024, and through which channels the two are expected to bear on firm value in an emerging market where the state remains a dominant owner. Design/methodology/approach: The study adopts a qualitative design that combines systematic document analysis of 18 regulatory and soft-law instruments issued between 2012 and 2024 with an integrative review of published empirical evidence on Vietnamese listed companies and secondary benchmark data from the ASEAN Corporate Governance Scorecard and a ten-year census of disclosure practices. Material was coded deductively against agency, stakeholder, legitimacy, signalling and institutional theory, and inductively for emergent themes. Findings: Vietnam’s regime moved through three phases: Mandated entry (2015 to 2017), soft-law consolidation (2017 to 2020) and statutory upgrading with climate alignment (2021 to 2024). Disclosure spread rapidly in breadth, yet depth lagged. Standalone reports rose only from about 1 percent to 7 percent of listed firms, GRI referencing stayed near 22 percent throughout the decade, and third-party assurance remained rare. Vietnam’s mean governance score in the 2024 regional assessment (60.15 points) sat 31 points below the ASEAN mean. The empirical literature reports a mostly positive association between disclosure and value, but the evidence is concentrated among large firms and is sensitive to how disclosure is measured. We argue that governance shapes value less through the volume of ESG disclosure than through its credibility, and we formalise this argument in a conceptual framework with five propositions. Originality/value: The paper offers the first decade-long, regulation-anchored synthesis of the governance, disclosure and value nexus in Vietnam. It distinguishes formal adoption from substantive practice and proposes a credibility-centred mechanism that can be tested once longitudinal, assurance-adjusted disclosure data become available.

title: HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT AND DIGITAL SKILLS AS DRIVERS OF LABOR MARKET ADAPTATION IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
summary: This thesis analyzes the contribution of human capital and digital skills to labor market adaptation in the digital economy. Based on systematic conceptual analysis, it distinguishes foundational digital literacy, occupation-specific competencies, and transferable analytical capabilities. The study examines how changing workplace tasks generate skills mismatches and why continuous training requires coordination between employers and education providers. A conceptual framework is proposed for linking competency assessment, modular learning, and employment outcomes. Recommendations focus on demand-oriented reskilling, verifiable skill acquisition, and inclusive access to lifelong learning.

title: Navigating digital transformation for inventory leanness through product and supply chain strategy
summary: Purpose This study examines why digital transformation has a non-monotonic effect on inventory leanness and how product diversification and supply-chain concentration condition this relationship. Design/methodology/approach The empirical analysis uses an unbalanced panel of 2,533 Chinese listed manufacturing firms and 19,299 firm-year observations from 2010 to 2023. Firm and year fixed effects are absorbed and conventional standard errors are reported in the primary models. Following Haans et al. (2016), the quadratic specification is treated as a parsimonious empirical approximation to a theory-derived marginal-effect pattern; the analysis tests endpoint slopes, the Lind–Mehlum joint U test, and Fieller confidence intervals; and evaluates conditional curvature, turning-point movement and shape-flip in the moderated models. Findings The findings reveal a U-shaped relationship between digital transformation and inventory leanness. Product diversification strengthens the curvature of this relationship, and this curvature-enhancing effect is further amplified by supplier concentration but weakened by customer concentration. Conditional analyses indicate that the complete U-shaped pattern depends on specific configurations, with limited shape reversals occurring only at the distributional tails. Practical implications Managers should distinguish exploration-related learning friction from the exploitation of retained digital routines. Product diversification raises the information-processing burden during early transformation but can create stronger inventory benefits after digital routines mature. Deep supplier coordination can reinforce these benefits through relation-specific digital assets, whereas dependence on a small number of powerful customers can limit portfolio-wide inventory optimization. Originality/value The study contributes by identifying two countervailing latent mechanisms – exploration-related learning friction and the exploitation of retained digital routines – that combine additively to generate a U-shaped relationship. It further shows how product complexity alters the curvature of this relationship and how supplier and customer concentration provide asymmetric boundary conditions. The analysis responds to methodological concerns in nonlinear research by separating curvature change, turning-point movement and shape-flip.

title: Accounting for the working conditions of social compliance auditors investigating modern slavery in supply chains
summary: Purpose This study explores the working conditions of social compliance auditors who investigate modern slavery in global supply chains. This issue is important for understanding how auditors' working environment shapes audits as a key mechanism for detecting modern slavery. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 32 interviews with actors involved in social compliance auditing, including auditors, certification bodies, NGOs and accreditation agencies. Drawing on labour process theory and the complex role of multi-principal employment networks, we analyse how the work of auditing, the objects of that work and the instruments that structure it organises control, dependency and risk across external modern slavery audits. Findings Our findings show that social compliance auditing can be intensive, under-resourced work in remote, often hostile settings, producing heightened vulnerability for auditors. We also find that auditors periodically face physical harm and managerial coercion, including intimidation, violence and efforts to manipulate or suppress critical findings precisely because those findings pose a threat to business interests when non-compliant labour practices are found. Nonetheless, we show how auditors draw on “buffers of culpability” which include micro-resistance, safety-driven adaptation and agentic use of informal tools, relationships and planning, to preserve some investigative integrity despite these adverse conditions. Originality/value Businesses are increasingly held accountable for labour conditions in their supply chains and rely on social compliance auditors to independently assess operating facilities, yet auditors' own working conditions and structural vulnerabilities remain poorly understood. We specify implications at both agentic (micro) and structural (macro) levels for the governance and reform of social compliance auditing in the context of fragmented and multi-principal employment networks.
